disease.name: IKK2 Deficiency
disease.description:
IKK2 deficiency (severe combined immunodeficiency due to IKK2 deficiency; immunodeficiency 15B) is an autosomal recessive inborn error of immunity caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in IKBKB, the gene encoding IkappaB kinase 2 (IKK2/IKKbeta), the catalytic kinase of the canonical NF-kappaB activation pathway. It was defined in infants of Northern Cree ancestry homozygous for the IKBKB frameshift duplication c.1292dupG, which abolishes IKK2 expression.
Mechanistically the disease is a signaling defect rather than a developmental block: T-cell and B-cell development is essentially normal and lymphocyte counts are preserved, but without IKK2 the canonical NF-kappaB pathway cannot be activated downstream of the T-cell receptor, B-cell receptor, Toll-like receptors, and inflammatory cytokine receptors. The consequence is a combined immunodeficiency in which circulating T and B cells are almost exclusively of naive phenotype, regulatory T cells and gamma-delta T cells are absent, and patients have hypo- or agammaglobulinemia despite normal lymphocyte numbers. Onset is in infancy with life-threatening viral, bacterial, and fungal infections and failure to thrive; hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the definitive treatment.

claim.name: Visual Impairment
claim.description: Progressive loss of vision is the primary clinical consequence of DR. Early DR is often asymptomatic, but macular edema and PDR-related complications cause significant functional impairment. state.snippet: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a major complication of DM and a leading cause of vision loss in working middle-aged adults.

disease.name: Diabetic Retinopathy
disease.description: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a progressive neurovascular complication of both type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus and a leading cause of preventable blindness in working-age adults worldwide. Chronic hyperglycemia drives retinal microvascular injury through oxidative stress, inflammation, and vascular dysfunction, leading to pericyte loss, blood-retinal barrier (BRB) breakdown, and ultimately to macular edema and pathological neovascularization. Disease progresses from nonproliferative stages (NPDR), in which retinal vessels are damaged but neovascularization has not yet occurred, to proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR), characterized by VEGF-driven abnormal neovascularization. Diabetic macular edema (DME), due to BRB breakdown with fluid accumulation in the macula, is the major cause of moderate vision loss and can occur at any stage. Contemporary management rests on systematic screening, glycemic and cardiovascular risk-factor control, intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy for center-involving DME, and panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) for high-risk PDR.

state.explanation: ICO guidelines establish DR as a leading cause of vision loss in working-age adults, making visual impairment the primary clinical outcome.
